name: Classical Computing
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Bits, Switches, and Certainty
lesson.summary: Introduces classical computing as computation built from bits in definite 0/1 states, manipulated by deterministic logic gates ,  the baseline every later idea in this book has to be measured against.
lesson.body:
Every computer you have ever used ,  a phone, a laptop, a data-center server ,  works by boiling all information down to a single kind of unit: the bit. A bit can be in one of exactly two states, conventionally labeled 0 and 1. Physically, this usually means a tiny circuit element is held at a low voltage or a high voltage, or a transistor is switched off or on. The device doesn't care whether you're storing a photo, a song, or a spreadsheet formula; underneath, it's all just long strings of 0s and 1s, and the hardware only ever has to reliably tell "low" from "high."

That reliability is the whole point of choosing two states rather than, say, ten. It's much easier to build a circuit that confidently distinguishes "definitely off" from "definitely on" than one that has to distinguish ten finely graded voltage levels without getting confused by noise. This robustness is why binary became the standard: it trades some representational density for near-perfect certainty about what state a bit is in at any moment.

Computation happens when you wire bits into logic gates ,  small components that take one or more bits as input and produce a bit as output according to a fixed rule. An AND gate outputs 1 only if both its inputs are 1. An OR gate outputs 1 if at least one input is 1. A NOT gate simply flips its single input. These gates are deterministic: given the same inputs, a gate always produces the same output, every single time, with no randomness involved. You can chain gates together to build more complex operations. For instance, wiring an AND gate and an XOR gate together the right way gives you a "half adder" that adds two single bits: 0 and 0 gives 0, 1 and 0 gives 1, but 1 and 1 gives 0 with a carry of 1 ,  which is exactly how you'd write "1 + 1 = 10" in binary, the carry bit shifting into the next column just like carrying a 1 when you add 9 + 1 in decimal. Scale this idea up ,  millions or billions of gates wired together ,  and you get everything from a calculator to a chip that renders a video game in real time.

The crucial property to hold onto is determinism. A classical computer's next state is completely fixed by its current state and the fixed rules of its gates; there's no genuine uncertainty about what a bit "really is" while the computation runs. This is precisely the assumption that later chapters will start to question, because it's the assumption quantum computing challenges.

It's also worth remembering that classical computing is not a static target. Decades of engineering have made classical hardware faster, cheaper, and more energy-efficient, and that improvement hasn't stopped. Any claim that a quantum approach is "better" has to be compared against this continually improving classical baseline, not against some outdated snapshot of what computers used to do.
